drills.q: Trace this: a = [1,2]; b = a; b.append(3); print(a). What prints, and why?
drills.a: [1, 2, 3]. b = a never copies — b is a second name bound to the same list object as a, so mutating via b is visible through a too.

drills.q: When, if ever, is `is` the correct operator to use instead of `==`?
drills.a: Only for singleton/identity checks: x is None, x is True, x is False, or comparisons against a sentinel object created specifically for that purpose. Never for general value comparison of ints, strings, or custom objects.

drills.q: Explain precisely why `grid = [[0]*3]*3` produces a grid where mutating grid[0][0] changes grid[1][0] and grid[2][0] as well.
drills.a: [0]*3 evaluates once, producing a single inner list object. The outer *3 builds a new outer list containing three references to that same inner object, not three independently constructed rows. So all three 'rows' are literally the same object, and mutating it through any one index is visible through all three.

drills.q: Write the correct way to construct a 3x3 grid of independent rows and explain why it avoids the aliasing bug.
drills.a: [[0]*3 for _ in range(3)] — a list comprehension re-evaluates its expression [0]*3 fresh on every one of its 3 iterations, so three distinct inner list objects are created instead of one shared object referenced three times.

drills.q: You do `shallow = copy.copy(original)` where original is a list of lists. Appending to shallow doesn't affect original, but appending to shallow[0] does. Explain both halves of this behavior.
drills.a: copy.copy creates a new OUTER list, so appending to shallow itself only changes the new outer container, leaving original's outer list untouched. But the elements inside shallow are the same object references as in original (only one level was copied), so shallow[0] and original[0] point to the identical inner list, and mutating it through either name is visible through both.

drills.q: How does copy.deepcopy correctly handle a self-referential list like `a = []; a.append(a)` without infinite-looping?
drills.a: deepcopy keeps a memo dict keyed by id() of objects currently being copied. It registers the newly created (still partially built) copy in the memo BEFORE recursing into the object's contents. When it encounters the same object id again mid-recursion, it returns the already-registered copy instead of recursing again, terminating the cycle correctly while preserving the self-reference in the result.

drills.q: Give two concrete situations where using copy.deepcopy is the wrong engineering choice, and what you'd do instead in each.
drills.a: 1) Only top-level isolation is actually needed (you'll only add/remove elements, never mutate nested elements) — use copy.copy instead, which is O(top-level size) versus deepcopy's O(entire reachable graph). 2) The object holds a live external resource (file handle, socket, DB connection, lock) — implement __deepcopy__ to keep that attribute shared or reconnect explicitly, since naively deep-copying a resource handle either raises or produces a broken duplicate.

drills.q: Implement __deepcopy__ for a TreeNode class with value, children, and parent attributes such that deep-copying a subtree does not walk upward through parent and copy the whole tree.
drills.a: def __deepcopy__(self, memo): new = TreeNode.__new__(TreeNode); memo[id(self)] = new; new.value = copy.deepcopy(self.value, memo); new.children = copy.deepcopy(self.children, memo); new.parent = self.parent  # deliberately shared, not deep-copied; return new. Registering in memo before recursing also keeps this safe if a node is reachable via multiple paths.

drills.q: Why does relying on `is` for integer comparison sometimes pass in unit tests and then fail in production with real data?
drills.a: CPython caches small integers in [-5, 256] as singletons, so is happens to agree with == for small literals used in tests. Once production values exceed 256 (a growing counter, a database-generated ID), they're typically separate objects even when equal in value, so is silently returns False where == would return True — no exception is raised, just a wrong answer.

drills.q: How does pandas 3.0's Copy-on-Write default (made the only mode as of the January 2026 release) relate to the shallow-copy aliasing bugs covered in this module, and what specifically changed for chained assignment?
drills.a: Pre-3.0, pandas indexing sometimes returned a view (memory shared with the original, like a shallow copy) and sometimes an actual copy, depending on undocumented internal memory layout, so chained assignment like df[df.x>0]['y']=1 could silently mutate the original or silently do nothing. Pandas 3.0 makes every operation behave as a logically independent copy (sharing memory lazily underneath until a write forces an actual copy), and chained assignment now raises explicitly instead of behaving unpredictably.
